clue.text: Informer has information to report

indicators.note: to report means to say out loud, so the word is taken by its sound

parts.note: someone who has information knows

explanation.surface: A police informant has something to pass on to the authorities.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to report' signals a sound-alike: KNOWS, said aloud, is the answer's sound.
explanation.definitionFit: In slang a police informant is a nose, someone who sniffs things out for the police.

clue.text: Customer's right defended by court

indicators.note: something defended by another is surrounded and protected by it, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a lien is a legal right to keep someone's property until a debt is paid

explanation.surface: A shopper's legal entitlement is upheld in court.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's after Customer stands for 'has', a link. A lien is a legal claim on property until a debt is settled.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym: a person buying goods or services from a business or professional is their customer.

clue.text: Old Bob with nurses clothing quietly disappears

parts.note: a bob was the old British shilling, abbreviated S

indicators.note: nurses clothing quietly means the nurses wrap around the quiet letter, as clothes surround a body

parts.note: nurses are carers
P (piano) is the musical marking for quietly

explanation.surface: An elderly man called Bob, kept company by nurses, slips away silently.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old Bob' reads as an elderly man, but a bob was slang for a shilling, the pre-1971 British coin, written S. 'clothing' puts P inside CARERS.
explanation.definitionFit: Scarper is British slang for run away or vanish quickly, so it means disappears.

clue.text: All the liquid is deadly

indicators.note: liquid means flowing and unfixed, so the letters are free to rearrange

explanation.surface: Every drop of this fluid is poisonous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'liquid' looks like part of the picture, but it is the anagram signal on ALL THE.
explanation.definitionFit: A direct synonym: both words describe something able to kill.

clue.text: Rat-arsed group breaks into chorus

indicators.note: the group breaks into the chorus word, so it sits inside it

parts.note: to chorus is to sing together
a team is a group

explanation.surface: A drunken gang suddenly starts singing together.
explanation.walkthrough: Rat-arsed is crude British slang for very drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: Steaming is also British slang for heavily drunk, so the two are synonyms.

clue.text: A Parisian on leave with journalist has not returned

parts.note: a Parisian says un for a
re means on, concerning
to quit is to leave
ED is short for editor, a journalist

explanation.surface: A Frenchman on holiday with a reporter has not come home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on leave' reads as a single phrase, a holiday from work, but the two words do separate jobs.
explanation.definitionFit: Love that is unrequited is not given back by the person loved.

clue.text: Star in Cannes barely gets work

indicators.note: barely means with the covering stripped, so the French word loses its first and last letters

parts.note: etoile is French for star, as said in Cannes

explanation.surface: A film star at the Cannes festival hardly gets any acting jobs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'barely' strips the outer E's from ETOILE, the French word for star.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym: hard labour or effort is toil.

clue.text: Fruity type of girl in size nines, going by air

definitions.meaning: a kind of small citrus fruit like a mandarin

definitions.text: girl in size nines, going by air
definitions.meaning: the heroine of the song Oh My Darling, whose shoes were number nine and who is known only through the tune

explanation.surface: A lively sort of girl in large shoes is flying somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going by air' sounds like a flight, but means known by a song: the American folk song Oh My Darling, Clementine says her shoes were number nine.
explanation.definitionFit: A small seedless citrus fruit; and the heroine named in the old folk song's title.

clue.text: Comedian appearing in English town near Clapton

indicators.note: near says the first name sits right beside the town name

parts.note: Eric Clapton is the guitarist, so his first name stands with him
Morecambe is a seaside town in Lancashire

explanation.surface: A comic is performing in an English town not far from Clapton.
explanation.walkthrough: Clapton reads as the London district, but it points to the guitarist Eric Clapton. Morecambe is a seaside town in Lancashire.
explanation.definitionFit: Half of Morecambe and Wise, the much-loved British TV comedy double act.

clue.text: Verne novel featuring Nemo's second appearance

indicators.note: the jumbled name features a letter, holding it inside
novel means new, so the author's name is given a new arrangement
second picks the second letter of the captain's name

explanation.surface: A Jules Verne book in which Captain Nemo turns up again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' rearranges VERNE into VENER; 'featuring' puts E, the 'second' letter of Nemo's, inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A veneer is a thin surface layer, hence an outward show or appearance hiding what lies beneath.

clue.text: Cat sits in pub, totally blissful

indicators.note: the retching word sits inside the pub word

parts.note: an inn is a pub
to cat is slang for vomit, which is to heave

explanation.surface: A cat lounging in a pub is perfectly content.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cat' looks like the animal but is the verb: to cat is British slang for to be sick, to heave.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: someone in heaven is in a state of complete bliss.

clue.text: Contour shows mother is out of shape

indicators.note: out of shape means bent from its form, so the letters are reformed

explanation.surface: An outline reveals that Mum has lost her figure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of shape' rearranges MOTHER IS.
explanation.definitionFit: On a weather map an isotherm is a contour line joining places at an equal temperature.

clue.text: Police scared a lot of priests

indicators.note: to police is to regulate and put in order, so the letters are reordered

explanation.surface: The police frightened many members of the clergy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Police' looks like a noun but is the anagram signal, as a verb, on SCARED A LOT.
explanation.definitionFit: Sacerdotal is a formal adjective meaning relating to priests or the priesthood.

clue.text: Bet on a horse that's out of commission

parts.note: laid is a past form of to lay, to bet
a jockey up is riding, on a horse

explanation.surface: A gambler has put money on a horse that can no longer race.
explanation.walkthrough: A rider is said to be 'up' when mounted on a horse.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: someone laid up is confined by illness or injury, out of action.

clue.text: He fights with oarsmen on boat

indicators.note: on here says the rowers come after the boat word, in an across answer

parts.note: a cruiser is a type of boat
an eight is a rowing crew of eight oarsmen

explanation.surface: A man goes into battle alongside a rowing crew aboard a vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: A cruiserweight is a boxer in the division between light heavyweight and heavyweight.

clue.text: A lot of you'll bond after revolution — if it's like this?

indicators.note: after revolution means the words are turned over, so their letters are rearranged
a lot of means most but not all, so one letter is dropped

explanation.surface: Political musing: people will unite after an uprising, provided it is peaceful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A lot of' drops one L, and 'after revolution' is the anagram signal; the definition leans on the whole clue, picturing a peaceful uprising.
explanation.definitionFit: Unbloody means without bloodshed, describing the sort of revolution that brings people together.

clue.text: One discovers knowledge preserved by old priest

parts.note: ex means former, old

indicators.note: the knowledge is preserved by the priest, held inside his letters

parts.note: lore is traditional knowledge

explanation.surface: Someone finds learning kept safe by a former clergyman.
explanation.definitionFit: An explorer travels to find unknown places, so one who discovers.

clue.text: Volcano here, blowing the front off public vehicle

indicators.note: blowing the front off removes the opening letter of the word here

parts.note: a bus is public transport

explanation.surface: A volcano near here has erupted and blasted the front off a bus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'blowing the front off' drops the H from HERE, leaving ERE.
explanation.definitionFit: Mount Erebus is an active volcano in Antarctica, on Ross Island.

clue.text: Small sun lamp

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for sun, as in Sunday
a lamp is a light

explanation.surface: A little sunlamp for the bedside.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym: slight means small in size or degree.

clue.text: Some stars from Die Hard engaged in speculation, after retiring

indicators.note: retiring means drawing back, so the whole is read backwards
the film words are engaged in the speculation word, held inside it

parts.note: spec is short for speculation, as in on spec
H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: A few film stars from Die Hard were involved in a speculative venture before stepping back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'engaged in' puts DIEH inside SPEC, giving SDIEHPEC; 'after retiring' reverses it. 'Some stars' looks like the film's actors.
explanation.definitionFit: Cepheids are pulsating variable stars whose period reveals their brightness, used to measure cosmic distances.

clue.text: Almost 70 fixed points in the spacetime continuum

indicators.note: fixed means mended or rearranged, so the letters are reordered
almost means not quite all, so the number word loses its last letter

parts.note: seventy is 70

explanation.surface: Sounds like Doctor Who: around seventy fixed moments in time and space.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Almost' cuts SEVENTY to SEVENT; 'fixed' rearranges it. 'fixed points' looks like one phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: In relativity an event is a single point in spacetime, located by place and time together.

clue.text: Po, the central character in Teletubbies, participated in games

indicators.note: the middle letter participated in the games, so it goes inside them

parts.note: polo and nim are both games

indicators.note: central character in picks the middle letter of the eleven-letter show name

explanation.surface: Po, the Teletubby at the heart of the show, took part in sports.
explanation.walkthrough: 'central character in' gives U from Teletubbies; 'participated in' puts it inside POLO plus NIM (a matchstick game). Po is a Teletubby but here the chemical symbol.
explanation.definitionFit: Po is the chemical symbol of the radioactive element discovered by Marie and Pierre Curie.

clue.text: Dagger from old non-Arab country

indicators.note: non-Arab says the country must lose AR, a standard abbreviation for Arab or Arabic

parts.note: Belarus is a country in eastern Europe

explanation.surface: A knife from an ancient land that is not in the Arab world.
explanation.walkthrough: 'non-Arab' removes AR (Arab) from BELARUS. 'Dagger' is the printed mark, not the weapon.
explanation.definitionFit: The obelus is the printer's dagger sign, used for footnotes, and the division sign.

clue.text: Druggie shooting up in Baltimore subway

indicators.note: shooting up says the hidden letters are read backwards
in says the letters sit inside the words that follow, spanning two of them

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: An addict injecting heroin on Baltimore's underground train.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shooting up' reads as injecting drugs, but in a down answer it means going upwards, read backwards; 'in' marks the run hidden in Baltimore subway.
explanation.definitionFit: A drug user is a druggie, a drug addict.

clue.text: Bad luck in Derby?

definitions.meaning: a British idiom for tough luck, said with little sympathy
Derby is a firm English cheese, so an example of a firm-textured cheese, with the query marking the example

explanation.surface: A losing bet on the Derby horse race.
explanation.walkthrough: The Derby is a famous English horse race, but Derby is also a cheese made in Derbyshire.
explanation.definitionFit: Tough luck, as a phrase of mock sympathy; and Derby is a firm-textured cheese.

clue.text: You can count on these at hotels regularly

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is taken

explanation.surface: A reliable feature you will find at hotels.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly' takes the 2nd, 4th, 6th and 8th letters of AT HOTELS.
explanation.definitionFit: Children count on their fingers and these other digits, so a playful definition of the feet's digits.
